title: Chest freezer: safe teardown
summary: A working chest freezer is worth far more whole: on an external thermostat it makes a very low-power fridge, and even dead it is an excellent insulated box. From a scrapped one take the thermostat, the compressor's start relay, overload and capacitor, the lights and the cord. Keep the refrigerant loop sealed (some newer ones use flammable R-600a), never drill the walls where the condenser runs, and mind the spring-loaded lid hinges.

steps.text: Decide first. If it runs, keep it whole and use it as a freezer, or as a low-power fridge on an external thermostat (build_chest_freezer_fridge). If it is dead, the cabinet is still an insulated box: keep that whole too and take only the small parts.

Read the rating plate (on an outside wall or the back) and note the refrigerant. R-600a and R-290 are flammable; R-134a is not; very old freezers may hold R-12. A flammable-refrigerant label or red-marked tubing also means hydrocarbon gas.
steps.warn: With a flammable refrigerant, keep flames, sparks and cigarettes away for the whole job. Hissing or oily stains mean the loop is already open: step back, air the area and read safety_refrigerant.

steps.text: Unplug it and keep the plug where you can see it. Empty it. If it has been off with food in it, expect rotten food, leaked juices and mould: wear gloves and a dust mask, bag the food and keep it away from living areas. Open the defrost drain plug to let any water out. Never chip frost with a knife or screwdriver: Danby warns that sharp tools used on frost can damage the refrigerant lines. From now on wait at least 5 minutes before you reach into the compressor compartment.
If you must move it, tape the lid shut, keep it upright, and lift it from the base with two people, never by the lid.
steps.warn: A 7 cu ft (197 L) freezer weighs about 32 kg (70 lb); bigger ones weigh much more, so add helpers or use a hand truck. If it lay on its back or side, stand it upright for about 6 hours before you run it. Take the tape off the lid once it is in place.

steps.text: Never drill, screw into or cut the outer walls, and never stab or scrape the inner liner. A chest freezer's condenser is wrapped around the case, so a screw or blade through the side can hit a refrigerant line.
steps.warn: A punctured line sprays refrigerant and oil: frostbite, eye injury, and fire with R-600a or R-290.

steps.text: Take off the compressor compartment cover at the back corner. Find the compressor's electrical parts: a start relay or starter pushed onto the compressor's pins, an overload, and, if there is one, a run capacitor nearby.
steps.warn: Don't touch any terminal yet: the capacitor may still hold a charge.

steps.text: Discharge the run capacitor with your resistor tool, holding the probe on each terminal for at least 10 seconds, then from each terminal to the metal frame (see safety_discharge_capacitor). Check your meter on a known source, measure DC volts across the terminals and to the frame (under 1 V), and check the meter again. Clip a jumper wire across the terminals.
steps.warn: Never short it with a screwdriver. If a reading stays above 1 V, discharge again and measure again.

steps.text: Pull the relay and overload off the compressor's pins. Keep the jumper wire across the capacitor's terminals until the capacitor is out, then unplug it, lift it out and twist a bare wire across its terminals. Tape the three parts together with a note of which freezer they came from.

Thermostat: pull off the dial knob, undo the screws of the control panel behind it and unplug the thermostat's wires. Its thin sensing tube runs into the cabinet. Draw it out only if it slides free, without kinking it. If it won't come, leave the thermostat in place.
steps.warn: Some thin tubes are refrigerant lines and look alike. Never cut, kink or pull any tube you can't trace back to the thermostat body.

steps.text: Take the power-on light and, on models that have them, the lid lamp, its socket and the lid switch: unplug each, then undo its screw or release its clips.

If you will leave the freezer behind, make sure no child can be trapped in it: Danby says to take the lid off before an old freezer is thrown away. First lift any plastic hinge covers and look at each hinge. If you can see or feel a spring, or you can't tell, leave the hinges and the lid alone, take the lock and catch off (next step) and keep the freezer out of children's reach. If the hinge is plain, with no spring, prop the lid fully open, have a helper take its weight, undo only the screws that fix each hinge to the cabinet, and lift the lid away. Leave the baskets in place.
steps.warn: GE says most chest freezer lids are under spring tension and to ask the maker for a safe way to remove one. Never take a hinge apart or undo the screws on the hinge body, and never let go of a propped lid. Keep fingers out of the hinge.

steps.text: If it has a key lock, take the lock and its catch off. Never fit a lock to a freezer, or to a cooler box made from one.

Only if the cabinet is being scrapped. First look at the gasket and the lid insulation: on a very old freezer, grey or white fibrous board, rope seals or papery wrap may be asbestos, so leave it (safety_asbestos_check). If it looks clear, pull the lid gasket out of its channel, then open the lid liner if you want its insulation.
steps.warn: Some lids are packed with loose fibreglass: wear gloves, long sleeves, goggles and an N95 or P2 mask. On a very old freezer, treat grey, papery or fibrous board as possible asbestos and leave it (safety_asbestos_check).

steps.text: Leave the compressor and every tube sealed. If you really need the compressor, use the crimp-first method in teardown_fridge_compressor, outdoors and away from any flame or spark.
steps.warn: Never drill, unbraze or heat a line on an intact loop, and never cut one except by that crimp-first method. Keep grinders and torches away from the tubing.

steps.text: Cut the mains cord off where it enters the cabinet and keep it whole with its plug. Keep the cabinet whole as an insulated box, and don't burn its foam. A freezer standing around with a lid that shuts is a child trap even for a few days (GE freezer manual): keep it where children can't get at it, and never fit a lock.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The running freezer.** Best of all. On an external thermostat a chest freezer makes a fridge that uses a fraction of an upright's power (build_chest_freezer_fridge).
- **The cabinet.** A ready-made insulated box: an icebox, a cool store with water jugs, or the body of a new cooler. The Danby DCF070B1WM holds 7.0 cu ft (197 L) and is 78 × 40 × 68 cm (30.8 × 15.8 × 26.8 in) inside (Danby DCF070B1WM page). Danby warns never to add a lock to the lid, and says to take the lid off before an old freezer is thrown away, because of child entrapment (Danby DCF070B1WM manual). GE says abandoned freezers are dangerous even if they sit for just a few days (GE freezer manual).
- **Thermostat.** A mechanical dial switch. The DCF070B1WM's is rated 250 V AC, 6(4) A (Danby DCF070B1WM parts). It can switch a cooler, a fermenting box or a small heater's relay, but its range is set for freezing, so check where it clicks before you rely on it.
- **Start relay, overload and capacitor.** The DCF070B1WM lists a relay/PTC starter (QP2-4.7H or JPQII-4.7), an overload (DRB21R61A1 or BT62-120) and a 6 µF, 250 V CBB65 capacitor (Danby DCF070B1WM parts). Keep them with their compressor: it won't start without its own.
- **Lights and switch.** The Frigidaire GLFC1526FW lists a lid lamp in a 25 W socket, a ramp-type lid switch and an amber signal light (Frigidaire GLFC1526FW parts); the Danby lists a green indicator light (Danby DCF070B1WM parts). The lid switch is a small spare limit switch.
- **Cord.** The Danby's is a 3-conductor SJT cord (Danby DCF070B1WM parts): an extension or appliance lead.
- **Compressor.** The Danby's is a UKT60YAX, 110–120 V, 60 Hz, R600a (Danby DCF070B1WM parts). Leave it sealed on an intact freezer (see safety_refrigerant). The only safe way out is the crimp-first method in teardown_fridge_compressor, outdoors and away from any flame or spark.

## Testing what you got out

- **Thermostat.** On the meter's continuity range at room temperature, turn the dial from off to coldest: it should click and show continuity (see test_continuity).
- **Capacitor.** See test_capacitor.
- **Overload.** Continuity at room temperature only shows it is closed. It can't show it will still open when it should: never heat it to test it, never bridge it, and never make a salvaged one the only protection.

## Variations

- **Refrigerant.** The Danby DCF070B1WM uses R600a (Danby DCF070B1WM parts), and Danby's manual warns of fire or explosion and says not to puncture the tubing (Danby DCF070B1WM manual). Frigidaire's 2004 catalog for the FFC0723DW0 names its series 134A, which looks like R-134a, but the catalog does not say so: read the rating plate (Frigidaire FFC0723DW parts). GE's 2001 freezer manual tells owners of an old freezer that used CFC refrigerant to have the CFC removed by a qualified servicer before disposal (GE freezer manual). The EPA notes hydrocarbon units carry a warning label and red tubing (EPA disaster guidance).
- **Starting parts.** Danby uses a separate relay and overload; Frigidaire lists a single compressor controller beside a 220 V run capacitor (12 µF on the FFC0723DW0, 15 µF on the GLFC1526FW0) (Frigidaire FFC0723DW parts; Frigidaire GLFC1526FW parts).
- **Lids.** GE says most chest freezer lids are under spring tension, calls for particular caution when removing one, and tells owners to contact the maker for a safe removal method (GE freezer manual). Both Frigidaire catalogs list the lid insulation as bulk fibreglass (Frigidaire FFC0723DW parts; Frigidaire GLFC1526FW parts), and the GLFC1526FW has a key lock (Frigidaire GLFC1526FW parts).
- **Drains.** The DCF070B1WM has a front-mounted drain (Danby DCF070B1WM page); its manual calls the outer part a drain cap (Danby DCF070B1WM manual).

## What to leave

- **The sealed loop:** compressor, the condenser wrapped round the case (GE exterior case warm), the evaporator, and the drier filter and process tube that Danby lists as part of it (Danby DCF070B1WM parts).
- **The wall foam.** It is bonded in, and getting it out means cutting the walls where the tubing runs.
- **Releasing refrigerant on purpose.** In the US it is illegal to knowingly vent it when getting rid of a freezer (EPA disaster guidance).
- **Burning the foam.** Don't.
